Siemens and NVIDIA Accelerate Lithography for Next-Generation AI Chipsby Daniel Nenni on 10-19-2026 at 6:00 am

View Profile

View Forum Posts

View Articles

Private Message

Categories: EDA, Lithography, Siemens EDA

Key takeaways ▼

Siemens has announced advances in its collaboration with NVIDIA to accelerate computational lithography, addressing a demanding step in manufacturing advanced AI semiconductors. By integrating NVIDIA’s cuLitho library with Siemens Calibre manufacturing software, the companies aim to make sophisticated photomask optimization practical at full-chip scale. Announced October 14, 2026, the integration delivers up to 12 times faster full-chip optical proximity correction workloads, according to Siemens.
The development addresses a fundamental manufacturing problem: the patterns engineers design do not automatically print accurately onto silicon. At extremely small dimensions, diffraction and other physical effects distort the projected image. Computational lithography predicts those effects and adjusts photomask geometries so the resulting wafer patterns more closely match the intended circuitry. NVIDIA describes the process as combining electromagnetic physics, photochemistry, computational geometry, and iterative optimization.
These calculations become more demanding as semiconductor features shrink. Manufacturers must account for increasingly complex interactions while controlling production variability. Siemens identifies the transition to high numerical aperture extreme ultraviolet lithography, known as High-NA EUV, as a particular challenge. Advanced approaches such as inverse lithography technology, or ILT, require substantial computing resources, potentially forcing compromises between optimization depth and delivery schedules.
ILT approaches mask creation by working backward from the desired wafer pattern to determine suitable mask shapes. Those shapes can include complex curves rather than conventional straight-edged geometries. NVIDIA identifies both ILT and curvilinear optical proximity correction as applications that benefit from accelerated computation, alongside modeling needed for future semiconductor scaling.
The reported performance gains require careful interpretation. Siemens cites simulation speedups ranging from at least 10 times to 17 times for selected workloads, alongside its headline figure for full-chip OPC. These measurements concern particular computational tasks. They do not establish an equivalent acceleration across the complete chip manufacturing process or guarantee identical improvements for every customer configuration.
The practical opportunity extends beyond completing an existing calculation sooner. Faster simulation can change which calculations engineers can afford to perform. A team facing a fixed deadline might use additional computing headroom to evaluate more candidate corrections, investigate difficult patterns, or examine a broader range of manufacturing conditions. The value comes from better decisions within the available schedule.
Siemens’ accompanying technical discussion describes computational lithography as a feedback loop connecting software models, photomask geometries, wafer exposure, and measurements of fabricated structures. It says acceleration can allow sophisticated optimization across larger portions of a design and reduce lengthy turnaround times from weeks to days. The company also identifies potential reductions in energy requirements and computing infrastructure footprint.
For manufacturers, those possibilities create an economic question alongside the technical one. More extensive analysis could help identify vulnerable patterns before expensive manufacturing commitments. However, the business case must include GPU infrastructure, software, integration, and operational costs. Useful customer comparisons would measure total turnaround time, correction quality, energy consumption, and the effort required to qualify an accelerated workflow.
The relevance to AI lies in the connection between computational capability and manufacturability. Designing a powerful processor is only part of delivering it commercially. Its physical patterns must also be produced consistently. Improvements in the software supporting that transfer can therefore contribute to the infrastructure behind future AI chips, even when they are less visible than advances in processor architecture.
There is also a reinforcing relationship: accelerated computing helps prepare more advanced semiconductors for manufacturing, and future semiconductors can provide additional computing capability. Siemens presents this cycle as an important mechanism for continued progress. Its significance will depend on maintaining accuracy while expanding the amount of useful optimization manufacturers can complete.
The collaboration matters because computing time constrains manufacturing choices. Reducing that constraint could give engineers greater freedom to apply advanced lithography methods, improve process robustness, and prepare complex AI silicon for production with fewer compromises.
